title: Barnes's three ways of playing clarinet: lead, vary, play under
summary: Barnes explains how he leads, varies, and plays underneath the trumpet, how Bechet, Louis and he played in that style, and how he rests his lips.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: That's right. Well me myself, I never do like a sax. At all. I like a clarinet. Now I play clarinet about three ways.
Three ways?
About three ways.
How is that?
I play clarinet in a manner, I lead. You understand? Now, if a trumpet is down, then I lead and I variate.
You lead and variate? Uh-huh.
Oh I see, you make any sense.
Lead and variate. Keep the lead going, but you're variating on the lead. Variate in there.
You see, now again, when that trumpet is playing, you hear me variating, playing underneath him.
Well, the second part is down low.
Yeah, I'm playing underneath him. Yeah, I remember how you do that. That's what I do. Now many men don't do that, they play one way. But I was like that.
Did most of the old time clarinet players play that way?
Well, no, I didn't find none of them played that. Most of them played in variate. Most all the clarinet played in variate. I don't care who they is.
All the time, huh?

Yeah. All the time in variate. Uh-huh. You never hold them, they come on nothing. And play, you know, produce. But like we played clarinet, like a man of us played clarinet, that was right to take Sidney, Louis, and myself. That's the man that I know. We played in that style. Right in that style. That's very stylish, very hard. And soft. Now if we're going to variate, it's soft. See, if you take a lead, you're taking heavy. See, now clarinet with a trumpet, you don't need that trumpet. When you raise, you can raise with them when you're going out.
Yeah, it's wonderful the way you do it. You're sort of thinking all the time what you're doing. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Men would play clarinet, they'd sit down, they'd play this what they played. Like Charlie, see Charlie McCurdy? Charlie wouldn't play but one way. Charlie played clarinet, he played clarinet. And he didn't want you to play nothing about clarinet.
When you say clarinet, you mean variate or? That's right. Variate, all the time. That's right. With or without a violin?

Yeah. He's right for me, see. What's him right for me? You understand, a man not playing music. But he's right for me, because he knows what he's doing. You see? Yeah. But I know what I'm doing, I'm going to work all around.
You're listening to the rest of the players and playing to suit them? Playing to suit them.
Yeah. Not playing to suit myself, I'm playing to suit them.
Yeah, I imagine that makes you a little more harder, all right?

It is harder in a manner of speaking, but many times you see me, I would take a rest. But I don't take a rest for that, I take a rest to come back very strong. See that's why I play. You don't take many rests though.
You had been a-

No, but I take enough rest to come back strong. It's a dry lip, say like a trumpet's here. See I play with trumpets already, they hold it back, let me dry my lips. Well I go and they're hard and hard, and they dry lips come back and I go on with them.
You say you keep your lips dry when you're playing?
No, no, they dry their lips. The trumpet player wants to- Yeah, he's my lip rest, he wants to dry lip rest. Yeah.
